taches.questions:
Image inpainting and local editing aim to modify a specified image region according to high-level instructions, such as a text prompt or a reference image, while ensuring coherence with the surrounding pixels. As an atomic operation for interactive image editing, it plays a fundamental role in applications ranging from object removal and insertion to creative content regeneration. Recent advances in text-to-image generation, particularly latent diffusion models (LDMs), have driven remarkable progress in inpainting and local editing. These methods perform diffusion in a low-dimensional, semantically compressed latent space and can generate complex, semantically coherent content guided by textual or structural cues.

However, latent local editing methods often struggle to maintain pixel-level consistency between synthesized regions and their surrounding context. The latent encoding and decoding inherent in these approaches introduces low-level compression errors, such as color and texture mismatches, that hinder pixel-level matching with the original background. When the edited region is pasted back into the source image, small visual differences tend to become more pronounced, producing visible mismatches at the boundaries. Such artifacts are a mixture of (i) chromatic shifts at editing boundaries, (ii) misaligned textures and inconsistent noise or grain patterns, and (iii) visible seams arising from content discontinuities. They typically persist across diverse inpainting and local editing methods and undermine both perceptual fidelity and practical usability.

Several approaches have been explored to mitigate these artifacts. Latent-space modifications integrate background information during generation or decoding: Asymmetric-VQGAN enriches the latent decoder with partial background inputs for context-aware decoding, and ASUKA introduces color augmentation during decoder training to simulate uniform chromatic discrepancies. Post-hoc pixel-level harmonization methods refine the synthesized region after generation: Poisson blending solves for seamless gradient transitions, while learning-based harmonization models such as DiffHarmony++ perform pixel-level adjustment. Yet subtle hue shifts, texture mismatches and content discontinuities often persist, because human perception remains sensitive to minute discrepancies at editing boundaries. Methods that rely on a specific latent space are also limited in how well they generalize to other latent representations and editing scenarios. Moreover, existing harmonization methods are typically designed for manually composited inputs in which a complete, well-defined foreground object is pasted into a clean background, whereas diffusion-based inpainting involves arbitrarily shaped masked regions with potentially complex semantics; many harmonization models also focus on adjusting the foreground appearance without explicitly enforcing background consistency.

This raises three open problems. First, subtle visual differences: how can persistent boundary artifacts caused by subtle but perceptible pixel-value differences or noise-pattern discrepancies be eliminated? Second, the complexity of local-editing artifacts: how can one handle artifacts that mix chromatic shifts, inconsistent noise or grain patterns, and content discontinuities? Third, generalization: how can a unified solution be developed that works across diverse latent diffusion models, latent spaces and editing applications such as inpainting, object removal and object insertion?

taches.questions:
Neural networks are increasingly deployed in settings where prediction confidence must be reliable. A classifier is said to be calibrated when its predicted confidence scores reflect the true likelihood of correctness, a property that is critical whenever predictive uncertainty informs downstream decisions. Modern neural networks, however, are often poorly calibrated despite high accuracy: they tend to be overconfident.

Calibration techniques fall into two categories. Intrinsic methods improve calibration during training, for example through loss modifications, data augmentation, or mixup. Post-hoc methods, including temperature scaling, Platt scaling, and isotonic regression, adjust model outputs after training without changing the weights. Post-hoc methods depend on held-out validation data and cannot correct uncertainty misestimation rooted in model internals, while some training-time regularizers have been reported to conflict with post-hoc calibration. Most intrinsic methods target the design of the loss function or regularization; the role of the optimization procedure itself, and of the trajectory it follows through parameter space, has received little attention as a lever for calibration.

Separately, geometric constraints such as orthogonality have been explored to improve deep networks, primarily for generalization and training stability, for instance through orthogonal convolutional filters, inter-layer gradient orthogonality, and orthogonalized descent schemes used to stabilize training. To our knowledge, the link between such geometric constraints on gradient-based optimization and calibration has not been investigated.

This raises several questions. Can a modification of the optimizer, with no change to the architecture or the loss, reduce overconfidence and improve calibration metrics such as expected calibration error and predictive entropy without harming accuracy? Would such a change remain compatible with standard post-hoc calibration, rather than conflicting with it? And can one explain, theoretically, by what mechanism the geometry of the descent direction would affect calibration?

taches.questions:
Diffusion models have made significant advances in video generation, particularly with DiT-based architectures, which greatly enhance visual quality. However, these models are often hindered by high memory usage, substantial computational costs, and long inference latencies, which limit their use in interactive applications. This has led to growing interest in more efficient and cost-effective generation strategies.

Approaches such as model distillation, pruning, and quantization have been widely adopted to accelerate inference. While effective, they require careful architectural design and retraining on large datasets, incurring high costs. Caching mechanisms, in contrast, offer a retraining-free alternative: the core idea is to reuse model outputs from specific timesteps during sampling to reduce redundant computation. Prior caching methods have used manually set rules for U-Net structures, have been extended to DiT-based image models, and, for video, have exploited patterns in attention differences across timesteps, redundancy in classifier-free guidance, or the correlation between timestep embeddings and model outputs combined with threshold-based indicators. Yet selecting which timesteps to cache, while balancing video quality and inference speed, remains an open problem in video generation.

Ideally, a lossless video acceleration method should meet two criteria: (i) high visual quality and (ii) consistency between accelerated and original videos. Existing cache-based methods maintain a certain level of visual quality, but they often introduce content deviations and loss of high-frequency details, increasing the risk of uncontrolled degradation.

Two limitations of prevailing caching strategies stand out. First, representative methods typically compute local errors between adjacent timesteps, often a relative L1 distance between consecutive model outputs, and apply a fixed threshold to decide whether to cache, implicitly assuming that all timesteps are equally important. However, the diffusion denoising process is temporally heterogeneous: noise levels and semantic richness vary across timesteps, with early steps shaping global structure and later steps refining details. A uniform threshold applied throughout the process can therefore lead to inaccurate caching decisions. Second, these methods focus on minimizing local differences between consecutive steps. While this may reduce short-term discrepancies, it overlooks how small errors accumulate and propagate over the sampling trajectory, potentially degrading both video quality and content consistency.

This raises several questions. How can caching decisions account for the way errors introduced at different timesteps accumulate and propagate over the sampling trajectory, rather than only the local change between adjacent steps? Given a fixed budget of full model evaluations, how should one decide which timesteps to compute and which to reuse so that accumulated degradation is controlled? Can such a caching schedule be determined without retraining and remain reliable across different inputs? Answering these questions matters for making high-quality video diffusion models practical in latency- and resource-constrained settings.

taches.questions:
The principle of "bias in, bias out" is widely recognised as a root cause of unfair outcomes in machine learning systems: models trained on biased data tend to learn, perpetuate, and often amplify such biases. The problem of biased data extends beyond training. Fairness-constrained training on biased data does not guarantee fairness on unbiased test sets, post-processing using biased validation data fails to ensure fairness at deployment, and fairness audits based on biased assessment data can be misleading and difficult to reverse.

Fairness metrics such as demographic parity and equal opportunity are functions of both the model and the data distribution, so unfair outcomes may be addressed either by adjusting the model or by altering the data distribution. Fair in-processing aims to construct a fair model under fairness constraints, whereas fair pre-processing alters the data. Early pre-processing work introduced heuristic reweighting for binary classification, adjusting the weight of instances from class i and group a by Pr(class i) Pr(group a) / Pr(class i, group a); this ignores the feature distribution and offers no fairness guarantee when combined with accuracy maximisation. Other work framed pre-processing as an optimisation problem balancing distance to the original distribution against group and individual fairness constraints, which may be infeasible when these notions are incompatible; still others address label bias through reweighting, propose fair adaptation based on causal models, or solve large-scale mixed-integer programs. Despite its heuristic nature, simple reweighing continues to perform well on standard benchmarks, and pre-processing remains widely used in fairness toolkits alongside in- and post-processing methods.

A common goal of all fair pre-processing methods is to find a data distribution close to the given one such that downstream models trained on it are guaranteed to be fair. Requiring this for downstream models optimised for multiple tasks leads to impossibility results: if every downstream classifier must be fair, the group-wise distributions must be nearly identical, which is impractical. A related line of work on fair Bayes optimal classifiers has shown that, under stylized data-bias models that inject under-representation and label bias into an unbiased distribution, the fair Bayes optimal classifier on the biased data can recover the Bayes optimal classifier on the unbiased distribution, on which the unconstrained optimum is already fair; but that line of research concerns the classifier rather than the distribution. Another approach seeks the nearest distribution in KL-divergence on which a Chernoff-information gap between the two group-conditional feature distributions vanishes; that problem is not known to be efficiently solvable, and guarantees stated as a Chernoff-information gap do not translate easily into standard metrics such as demographic parity or equal opportunity.

This leaves several open questions. Can one characterise target data distributions on which utility-maximising downstream models, whatever performance metric is eventually used, are guaranteed to be exactly group-fair, so that no fairness-utility trade-off exists, without forcing the group-conditional distributions to be identical, and in a form that can be checked efficiently? Given a distribution that lacks this property, how can one find the nearest distribution that has it, can this be done efficiently, and do guarantees obtained on the target carry back to the original distribution? Can such a target indicate in which direction to move a distribution so as to improve fairness without sacrificing, or even while improving, accuracy? Finally, steering the internal representations and generations of large language models is an active area with limited theoretical grounding: existing approaches, such as aligning the first two moments of representations or sampling steering vectors from a Gaussian distribution over concept vectors, lack provable fairness guarantees on the model output. Can a principled, fairness-guaranteeing notion of a target distribution guide such steering so that it reduces group disparities and works equally well across different groups?

taches.questions:
The emergence of reasoning models such as OpenAI's o1 and DeepSeek-R1 marks a significant advance in large language model (LLM) reasoning. A key driver of this progress is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), in which a rule-based checker rewards a response solely for the correctness of its final answer, typically optimized with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Nevertheless, RLVR continues to face the classic exploration-exploitation dilemma because of the exploitative nature of its objectives: policies tend to over-emphasize exploitation of high-reward trajectories, leading to entropy collapse, diminished exploratory capacity, and reduced final performance. Reduced exploration may drive the policy to overfit to the training distribution rather than discover generalizable reasoning patterns, so that gains on in-distribution data need not carry over to out-of-distribution problems.

One plausible account of entropy collapse is a self-reinforcing loop. As entropy falls, the policy forms increasingly confident beliefs about solutions, yielding a response distribution with multiple, imbalanced modes: several plausible reasoning behaviors exist for a given question, but one mode receives more probability mass. If rollouts predominantly sample this dominant mode and receive positive feedback, the policy further amplifies it while suppressing alternatives, which accelerates the collapse. Crucially, such a loop can impede the discovery of alternative, potentially superior reasoning strategies, causing local optima and poor generalization.

Recent efforts to improve exploration in RLVR largely fall into two categories: objective-level modifications and indiscriminate exploration. Approaches such as increasing the sampling temperature or adding entropy regularization flatten the output distribution uniformly; while this increases stochasticity, it does not shift probability mass away from dominant behaviors, since the dominant mode remains the most likely to be sampled even after flattening. A widely adopted objective-level approach, DAPO, raises the upper clipping threshold so that low-probability trajectories face fewer restrictions during training, and relaxing rewards with Pass@k similarly admits more low-probability trajectories. Yet these tweaks leave the rollout dynamics unchanged: during rollouts, the policy can remain confined to dominant modes and keep sampling previously visited high-probability regions, sustaining the self-reinforcing loop.

This raises the central question: how can a policy be made to explore plausible behaviors beyond its dominant mode during rollout, so as to break the self-reinforcing loop that drives entropy collapse, without destabilizing training, degrading generation quality, or substantially increasing computational cost? Answering it requires understanding whether more targeted exploration translates into better reasoning accuracy and better generalization to harder and out-of-distribution problems.

taches.questions:
Accurately estimating the state of Earth's atmosphere is essential to all aspects of society, from protecting food supplies to routing flights and optimizing renewable power generation, and there has been much interest in machine learning weather and climate prediction systems able to model the evolution of the atmosphere. However, many atmospheric processes are too detailed for current models to simulate directly. Shallow cumulus clouds, for example, generally span less than a kilometer, cover as much as 40% of the Earth's surface, form at altitudes below about 2000 m as the first cloud layer above the ground, and play a central role in controlling the Earth's temperature. Because they are small and short-lived, weather and climate simulators cannot resolve them; instead, hand-crafted parameterizations approximate their aggregate effect on temperature, moisture and winds on a much coarser grid, and these approximations are a major source of error in both day-to-day forecasts and long-range climate projections. Machine-learning systems such as GraphCast, Pangu-Weather and Aardvark inherit the problem, since they train on reanalysis data produced by the same physics-based models and operate at kilometer and hourly scales.

Developing better, higher-resolution models and assessing their impact requires detailed observations of individual clouds over their whole lifetime: the three-dimensional distribution of liquid water content, its column integral (the liquid water path), cloud base and cloud top heights, and the winds that advect the clouds. Such observations are not easily obtained with current systems. High-resolution satellite imagery has a revisit time of several days, while scanning radar and in situ aircraft measurements provide high detail but only for a small part of a cloud, lacking the larger context. Learned retrieval methods developed for satellite imagery, such as 3DeepCT and VIP-CT, implicitly learn camera geometry from small-scale synthetic datasets and assume near-orthographic, unobstructed views; earlier work with ground-based stereo cameras recovers geometric properties such as cloud base height but not physical quantities such as liquid water content. Moreover, no instrument provides dense three-dimensional ground truth of cloud water content at the resolution and scale of interest, which makes both learning and validating such retrievals difficult.

The open question is therefore whether, and how, the full four-dimensional physical state of shallow cumulus clouds (three-dimensional liquid water content and height-resolved horizontal winds) can be retrieved with accuracy, at a spatial and temporal resolution fine enough to resolve individual clouds across their life cycle, over an area large enough to capture their context, using low-cost and scalable sensing.

taches.questions:
The transformer has become the cornerstone of modern deep learning, powering advances in natural language processing, computer vision, speech and audio processing, and multimodal learning. At the core of the transformer is the self-attention mechanism, which effectively captures dependencies among sequential elements. However, this mechanism is inherently position-agnostic and permutation-invariant. Positional information is crucial in learning semantics because it encodes sequential dependencies analogous to a directional causal structure, as opposed to the undirected associations captured by self-attention.

To inject positional information into the transformer architecture, a plethora of strategies have been proposed to generate positional encodings that are integrated with contextual embeddings. These include fixed sinusoidal functions, trainable absolute or relative positional encodings, and more recent rotary positional encodings (RoPE). Notably, these methods generally assume a natural, inherent ordering in the data, such as the sequence of words in a sentence or the spatial arrangement of image patches; even recent variants that improve extrapolation to longer contexts assume a predefined sequential order among tokens.

This assumption breaks down for many real-world datasets, where rows represent independent observations, columns represent non-sequential features, and entries capture the quantity or state of each feature for a given observation. For example, in the biomedical sciences, multi-omics data such as transcriptomics and proteomics measure gene and protein expression levels within samples. The expressions of genes and proteins lack a predefined sequence, despite their intricate causal order. Similarly, economic studies often involve non-sequential but causally linked economic indicators collected across different regions or countries. Existing positional encoding methods therefore struggle to capture these underlying causal structures, limiting the applicability of transformers to such data.

Some preliminary efforts have emerged within specialized domains. In single-cell transcriptomics, transformer-based foundation models seek to generate distributed gene representations from large corpora of scRNA-seq datasets. To impose a pseudo-order on genes, some of these models organize trainable gene embeddings into sequences based on their expression levels, while others use pretrained, static gene embeddings derived from gene co-expression data as pseudo-positional encodings. These encodings capture association patterns or superficial relationships based on relative expression, and a critical limitation is that they neglect the underlying causal structure among genes.

The open problem is therefore: given a set of non-sequential yet causally related features and a tabular measurement dataset recording the quantity of each feature in each observation, how can positional encodings for the features be derived from the data so that they reflect the latent causal structure among the features, eliminating the need for a predefined feature ordering, and how can such encodings be integrated into a transformer's self-attention so as to improve the resulting feature-level and observation-level representations? The problem is challenging because the causal structure among features is hidden and must be inferred from observational data in which dependencies may be nonlinear; because the directed, acyclic nature of a causal graph, including how strongly pairs of features are causally related and how causally general or specific each feature is, has no obvious counterpart in conventional sequential positions; and because measurement data are often subject to measurement errors, so that the estimated causal structure, and any positions derived from it, may be perturbed.

domains: privacy-driven unlearning of personal information in LLMs

taches.questions:
Privacy regulations and copyright laws (e.g. the GDPR) necessitate the ability to selectively remove data from machine learning models, including Large Language Models (LLMs). While complete retraining without specific data can be optimal for information removal, it is infeasible at scale given the high computational costs of training LLMs. This motivates the need for machine unlearning techniques that erase specific information while preserving a model's broader capabilities.

Recent methods have demonstrated early progress in LLM unlearning, either via refusal fine-tuning or via gradient ascent and preference optimization on ground-truth sequences, yet they introduce severe unlearning-utility trade-offs and lack deeper theoretical analysis and robustness. Moreover, these methods optimize directly on the private sequences they seek to remove by incorporating them into their fine-tuning data. This is counterintuitive: it risks reinforcing exposure to sensitive data and contradicts the principle of minimizing its use. This dependency on unlearning targets may also introduce side effects that remain poorly understood, such as enabling adversaries to elicit data after unlearning. In many practical deployments, the original data may also be unavailable, restricted or impossible to share, one may not know which training samples gave rise to an output requiring unlearning, or no unique ground-truth forget sequence may exist. Evaluating unlearning in LLMs is itself an open challenge: most current evaluations assess whether a model avoids generating specific unlearning targets, but often overlook residual information leakage.

A seemingly unrelated line of work studies iterative retraining, where generative models are repeatedly trained on their own outputs. This can cause information loss in the model's output distribution and eventually lead to distribution collapse (model collapse), a phenomenon largely regarded as a bug in the LLM learning landscape; theoretical work has derived conditions under which collapse occurs, and mixing synthetic with original data has been shown to avoid it. There are notable parallels between the unlearning challenge and this loss of information. This raises the following research question: can the principles underlying model collapse be leveraged to develop principled approaches for machine unlearning?

Concretely, the problem is empirical machine unlearning for LLMs, defined as removing specific information from model outputs (for example, the answers to sensitive questions) without retraining from scratch and without requiring access to the ground-truth responses to those questions, while preserving the model's utility on all other queries. Doing so is challenging: the distributions one would like to alter are distributions over entire sequences, while LLMs only expose next-token distributions; unlearning is typically studied for question answering, where answers to forget questions must be removed while performance on retain queries is preserved; and specifying a well-formed target distribution to converge to is non-trivial without access to a model that has never been trained on the data, which usually requires expensive retraining. A principled approach should come with a theoretical account of why it removes the targeted information, and should remove it robustly, without unintended side effects on the model's behaviour outside the unlearning context.

taches.questions:
The current state of the art in generative modeling involves learning dynamics between a known source distribution, such as a standard Gaussian, and a target distribution from which many samples are available. When the dynamics are based on an ordinary differential equation (ODE), the model learns a vector field connecting the two distributions; when they are based on a stochastic differential equation (SDE), the score function, or both the score and the vector field, are learned, and any such SDE can be rewritten as a probability flow ODE. These methods perform very well across images, video, audio and molecular data, but generating samples is expensive because it requires integrating an ODE, and they generally do not learn optimal transport maps, which are often essential for unpaired data translation.

To address the cost of sampling, consistency models accelerate score-based approaches, while Rectified Flows aim to learn straight vector fields that can be integrated in a single step. Rectified Flows iteratively update couplings: at each iteration a vector field is trained with the conditional flow matching loss on the current coupling, and the next coupling is obtained by integrating the learned ODE from the source samples. Repeated rectifications can accumulate errors, and it remains theoretically unclear whether one or two rectifications suffice under general conditions: some works suggest that one rectification may be enough, a claim that two suffice was later retracted, and no formal proof exists. Parameterizations based on input-convex neural networks can in theory guarantee optimal couplings for noiseless interpolants but are difficult to optimize in practice. Schrödinger Bridge Matching learns both forward and backward vector fields using noisy interpolants, approximating entropic optimal transport; this can improve stability and mitigate error accumulation, but requires training two networks per iteration.

A flow matching objective can have several minimizers, and which one stochastic optimization actually reaches is not determined by the loss value alone. The variance of the Monte Carlo gradient of the loss is a natural lens on which solutions the loss landscape favors, and a common belief in the flow matching literature is that gradient variance originates primarily where straight-line interpolants intersect. It is not established when gradient variance is actually informative about the quality of a learned vector field, nor how it depends on the pairing between source and target samples (random, optimal, or merely straight), on the training regime, and on the class of vector fields considered.

These questions bear directly on memorization. Memorization and generalization in generative models have been studied extensively, with privacy and copyright infringement among the key concerns, but most studies sample source and target points independently. In Rectified Flows each training target has a deterministic counterpart in the source, so the appropriate notion changes: given a finite deterministic training set of pairs, memorization occurs if integrating the learned vector field from a training source returns exactly its paired target, reproducing the training coupling. This raises a central question for rectified-flow training: when the interpolating lines of different pairs intersect, so that the pairing cannot in principle be read off the interpolant, does training still lead to a well-defined transport, or can the objective be minimized by a field that reproduces arbitrary training pairings at inference? If deterministic integration simply recovers the original pairings, what value is added by learning a new vector field, and under which training regimes does a flow-based model generalize toward a better transport rather than reproduce its training couplings?

taches.questions:
Diffusion and flow matching models have become the dominant method for visual generation, delivering compelling image quality and diversity. However, these models rely on a costly denoising process for inference, which integrates a probability flow ODE over multiple timesteps, each step requiring a neural network evaluation. The inference cost of such models is commonly quantified by the number of function (network) evaluations (NFEs), and despite the progress in advanced ODE solvers, high-quality sampling typically requires over 10 steps due to inherent ODE truncation error, making it computationally expensive.

To reduce the inference cost, diffusion distillation methods compress a pre-trained multi-step model (the teacher) into a student that requires only one or a few network evaluation steps. Existing distillation approaches avoid ODE integration by taking one or a few shortcut steps that map noise to data, where each shortcut path is predicted by the student network (a shortcut-predicting model). This creates a format mismatch: the teacher predicts flow velocities, whereas the student predicts a shortcut towards denoised data. Learning these shortcuts is a significant challenge because they cannot be directly inferred from the teacher model, which necessitates complex training methods.

Early work directly regresses the teacher's ODE integral in a single step, but regressing the clean data with an l2 loss tends to produce blurry results. Progressive distillation methods improve on this via a multi-stage process that progressively increases the student's step size by regressing the previous stage's multi-step outputs with fewer steps, yet this introduces error accumulation. Consistency-based models implicitly impose a velocity-based regression loss, but the flow velocity of a shortcut-predicting student must be constructed implicitly using either inaccurate finite differences or expensive Jacobian-vector products; their quality is still limited by the accumulation of velocity errors into the integrated shortcut, and in practice they are often augmented with additional objectives, further complicating training. Distribution matching approaches use score matching and adversarial training to align the student's output distribution with the teacher's: variational score distillation (also known as distribution matching distillation) achieves high quality but risks diversity loss due to mode collapse, while GAN-style objectives balance quality and diversity but can cause style drift. Their common reliance on auxiliary networks introduces additional tuning complexity and may lead to stability issues at scale. In turn, such sophisticated training often leads to degraded image quality from error accumulation or to compromised diversity due to mode collapse, i.e., a quality-diversity trade-off.

The open problem is therefore how to obtain few-step generators, needing only one or a few network evaluations, whose distillation from a multi-step flow teacher is simple, stable and scalable to large models, that limit error accumulation along the generation trajectory, and that retain both the teacher's image quality and its sample diversity, rather than trading one for the other, without giving up the speed advantage of few-step sampling.

taches.questions:
The past few years have witnessed rapid progress in reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs). This began with reinforcement learning from human feedback, which aligns pre-trained LLMs with human preferences, followed by reasoning-oriented RL that enables LLMs to produce long chains of thought. More recently, agentic RL aims to train LLMs for agentic capabilities such as tool use, long-horizon planning, and multi-step task execution in dynamic environments.

Alongside these developments, off-policy RL has been attracting growing interest. In the "era of experience", LLM-powered agents need to be continually updated through interaction with the environment. Practical constraints in real-world deployment and the complexity of LLM-RL infrastructure often render on-policy training impractical: rollout generation and model training can proceed at mismatched speeds, data might be collected from different policies, reward feedback might be irregular or delayed, and the environment may be too costly or unstable to query for fresh trajectories. Moreover, in pursuit of higher sample efficiency and model performance, it is desirable to go beyond the standard paradigm of independent rollout sampling, e.g., via replaying past experiences, synthesizing higher-quality experiences based on auxiliary information, or incorporating expert demonstrations into online RL, all of which incur off-policyness.

However, the prominent algorithms in LLM-RL, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), are essentially on-policy methods: as modern variants of REINFORCE, their fundamental rationale is to produce unbiased estimates of the policy gradient, which requires fresh data sampled from the current policy. PPO and GRPO can handle a limited degree of off-policyness via importance sampling, typically with token-wise probability ratios that are clipped, but classical policy improvement guarantees require that the current policy remains sufficiently close to the behavior policy. Truly off-policy LLM-RL often demands ad-hoc analysis and algorithm design; worse still, as existing RL infrastructure is typically optimized for REINFORCE-style algorithms, its support for specialized off-policy RL algorithms could be limited.

Several recent practices also sit uneasily with the standard policy-gradient view. GRPO-style algorithms combine importance-sampling weights with clipping, yet it is unclear which of these ingredients actually matters when learning from stale data. Recent algorithms such as Kimi's Online Policy Mirror Descent (OPMD) and Meta's Asymmetric REINFORCE (AsymRE) come with their own, separate rationales. Data-weighting heuristics, such as strategically discarding some negative samples or up-weighting high-reward responses, violate the assumptions of policy gradient theory and often require ad-hoc analysis.

This raises several questions. Is on-policy sampling truly a prerequisite for REINFORCE-style algorithms that, like GRPO, sample multiple responses per prompt and use the within-group mean reward as a baseline, and how should such algorithms be understood when the training data come from older, delayed, or otherwise different policies? What general principles should guide adapting them to truly off-policy settings? And what are the actual roles of importance sampling, clipping, regularization, and data weighting in making these algorithms work under off-policyness? Answering these questions would enable principled, infrastructure-friendly algorithm design for off-policy RL in LLMs.

taches.questions:
Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve exceptional performance across a wide range of Natural Language Processing tasks. However, recent advances in prompting techniques, such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), inevitably increase input length, introducing two key challenges when deploying LLMs in long-context scenarios: (1) computational cost, as the quadratic complexity of the attention mechanism in Transformers leads to inefficiency with long sequences; and (2) information redundancy, where the presence of redundant content degrades model performance.

Context compression has emerged as a promising way to address these challenges by significantly reducing input length and eliminating redundancy. Existing prompt compression methods mainly fall into two categories: task-agnostic and task-aware context compression. LLMs typically allocate attention to only a small subset of query-relevant tokens. Consequently, task-agnostic methods, which compress the context without considering the input query, inevitably lose or dilute relevant information, especially at high compression rates.

Task-aware methods, in contrast, include the query in the compression process and preserve information according to its relevance, through query-guided strategies such as merging, deletion or summarization. However, they rely solely on relevance as a compression criterion and ignore the inherent redundancy of natural language. This leads to the retention of highly similar relevant content, and such over-similarity can mislead the LLM into producing erroneous outputs, since relevance does not guarantee correctness. The issue is amplified in long-context scenarios, where different segments carry different information value and should be compressed at different rates. Existing mechanisms for dynamically allocating compression rates are limited: they either follow predefined linear rules that lack adaptability, rely on model-internal understanding that is task-agnostic and may ignore query-relevant content, or set compression rates based solely on relevance, assigning lower compression to highly relevant content. None of them accounts for semantic redundancy among compression units, which leads to the repeated retention of similar information and compromises both compression effectiveness and information diversity. KV-cache compression offers another route, but it requires the compression model and the response model to be identical and needs model-specific modifications for different KV-cache structures.

This raises the research question: how can we retain query-relevant information while identifying and eliminating semantic redundancy among compressed representations, especially under high compression rates, so as to jointly optimize relevance and diversity?

taches.questions:
World models aim to learn state abstractions and action-conditioned dynamics that capture the evolution of high-dimensional observations, along with auxiliary information (e.g., rewards, skills), for decision-making tasks. Recent advances have demonstrated their effectiveness in downstream applications such as robotics and autonomous driving.

One of the central challenges for world models is to extract low-dimensional, structured latent representations from high-dimensional observations, which often display high complexity and variability across both semantic and dynamic aspects. On the dynamics side, latent spaces often contain underlying structures, and prior work imposes structural priors to learn compact latents that encourage disentanglement and capture relational or compositional patterns. On the semantics side, pre-trained visual features have been leveraged to better encode rich content and improve fidelity. Collectively, these approaches learn compressed, structured representations of high-dimensional perceptual data to support downstream decision making. However, it remains unclear to what extent such compression and structure are necessary and sufficient for downstream policy learning.

This raises the question of which types and degrees of decomposition structure make latent representations effective for efficient and generalizable policy learning. Real-world settings exhibit substantial variability in both visual appearance and dynamic interactions, often involving multiple objects with diverse attributes. Real-world dynamics are heavily influenced by rich interactions among objects, such as collisions, containment, stacking, and physical forces like friction or gravity, which collectively determine the evolution of the environment. Yet most object-centric reinforcement learning methods factor the state by individual objects while leaving the interactions among them implicit. Open questions therefore include whether and how objects, their interactions, and the attributes that govern these interactions should be represented in a world model learned from high-dimensional observations; whether such structure improves sample efficiency on long-horizon tasks that require completing sequences of sub-skills; and whether it supports generalization to unseen combinations of object attributes, objects, and skills.

taches.questions:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across a wide range of general-purpose tasks, including question answering, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. To further enhance their effectiveness in specialized applications, practitioners often perform additional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on domain-specific data. This enriches the model with domain knowledge and yields substantial gains on domain-specific tasks, and SFT has thus become a standard paradigm for adapting LLMs to real-world deployment scenarios.

However, recent studies have reported that fine-tuning LLMs on domain-specific datasets can substantially impair their general capabilities. For example, performing SFT on open LLMs with data from specialized domains is often reported to cause significant drops on general-purpose benchmarks that assess core capabilities like mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following. This widely held belief in an unavoidable trade-off between domain adaptation and general capability calls for a closer examination of domain-specific SFT: is the degradation intrinsic to fine-tuning on a narrow distribution, or does it depend on how the fine-tuning is carried out?

The problem can be framed within continual learning, where a model must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned capabilities and avoiding catastrophic forgetting. Existing approaches are either data-dependent, assuming access to part of the earlier training data, or data-oblivious, relying only on the pre-trained model. The data-oblivious setting is particularly realistic for LLMs, since proprietary or large-scale pre-training and post-training corpora are usually inaccessible, yet it remains relatively underexplored for LLMs. Data-oblivious strategies developed for earlier models include regularization that keeps the fine-tuned parameters close to their initialization (e.g., L2 penalties), averaging the weights of the pre-trained and fine-tuned models, restricting updates to a low-rank subspace (LoRA), and reweighting the loss of easy and hard training samples, as proposed for vision tasks. LLMs, however, differ substantially from earlier architectures in scale, pre-training regimes, and emergent capabilities, which makes their adaptation dynamics distinct, and it is unclear how well these ideas transfer.

This raises several open questions. Under which training conditions does domain-specific SFT severely degrade general capabilities, and under which can strong target-domain performance be reached while largely preserving them? What mechanism governs how fitting a new, narrow data distribution changes the model's fit on distributions it already models well, and which parts of the domain-specific training data drive this change? Finally, when degradation persists, which data-oblivious mitigation strategies offer the best balance between domain gains and the preservation of general capabilities, and can a principled strategy do better?
